title: Titles in name only
translation: The "nominal vice-governor", a title with no duties and no pay, wasn't the only one of its kind. There were nominal provincial clerks too. You'll find them in the Seiji Yōryaku.
original: {揚名介|やうめいのすけ}に{限|かぎ}らず、{揚名|やうめい}{目|さくわん}といふものあり。
{政事要略|せいじえうりやく}にあり。
literal: Not limited to the nominal vice-governor, there is also a thing called the nominal clerk.
It is in the Seiji Yōryaku.

notes.text: {揚名介|やうめいのすけ}: a vice-governor of a province in name only. The 1925 edition glosses it as 'a vice-governor with the title but no duties and no salary'. The word is famous from the 'Yūgao' chapter of the Tale of Genji, where it describes the owner of a house, and later readers of Genji argued about what it meant.

{目|さくわん}: the fourth and lowest of the four ranks of a provincial office: governor ({守|かみ}), vice-governor ({介|すけ}), secretary ({掾|じよう}) and clerk. The edition gives the reading さくわん (modern さかん). 'Clerk' in the translation is only an approximation.

The Seiji Yōryaku, a large collection of laws and administrative precedents. The 1925 edition says it was compiled by Koremune no Tadasuke ({允亮|ただすけ}) in the reign of Emperor Ichijō (around 1000). Only part of it survives.
This section and the ones around it are short notes on old words, offices and customs, each with its source. Compare sections 197 and 199–205.
